points.title: Consistently high return on total capital (12% or better)

points.title: Is revenue growth accelerating or decelerating? Did profits improve?

points.value: Company I - Durable Competitive Advantage - Per-share earnings are consistently positive and the latest year is at or above the prior year: the 'perfect situation' Buffettology looks for.
points.note: Exhibit A (the two images embedded in the Analyze sheet).

points.title: Do earnings show a strong upward trend?
points.formula: 10Y EPS growth rate  =  ((EPS[n]/EPS[0])^(1/n) - 1) * 100     [average of YoY growth % as a cross-check]
points.value: Per-share earnings compounded at 13.28% a year over the available 11-year span, against a risk-free rate of 6.8%.
points.note: The original statement5.py printed the MEAN OF THE RAW EPS RUPEES as the 'growth rate' (e.g. '10-year average EPS growth rate is: 150%' for a stock with EPS of 150). The correct figure is the compound growth rate shown above.

points.title: Are share prices and book value on the rise?
points.formula: Current Price > earliest comparable price   AND   Book Value growth rate > 0
points.value: Share price is above its level 10 years ago; book value is growing.

points.title: Earnings-per-share growth-rate test (5 year vs 10 year)
points.formula: 5Y EPS growth rate  vs  full-span EPS growth rate: pass if 5Y >= 12% (competitive benchmark), or 5Y >= full-span with positive growth (acceleration test), or 5Y Net Profit CAGR >= 12% with EPS growth positive (IPO-dilution rescue)
points.value: 5Y EPS CAGR 20.31% against the full-span CAGR of 13.28% (5Y Net Profit CAGR 21.55%). Earnings growth MEETS the >=12% competitive benchmark or the acceleration test.
points.note: Summary!D30 compared the two values as TEXT ('5.48 %' vs '0.44 %'), which compares alphabetically. Here they are compared as numbers, and a >12% 5Y CAGR passes outright.

points.title: Is revenue growth accelerating or decelerating? Did profits improve?
points.formula: Accelerating if 5Y Revenue CAGR > full-span Revenue CAGR (with positive growth); pass outright if the 5Y or full-span Revenue CAGR >= 12%; 'Decelerating' + profits improved if 5Y EPS growth > full-span EPS growth
points.value: Decelerating, Profits improvedDecelerating, Profits improved
points.note: A company compounding revenue at 12%+ across ANY available span passes this checkpoint - a short listed history (e.g. a recent IPO) is no longer reported as 'Insufficient data'.

points.title: Consistently earning a high return (15% or better) on equity
points.formula: GEOMEAN(ROE[0..9])  >=  15%   (12% for banks and other financial institutions)
points.value: 10-year geometric-average return on equity of 12.16% (above the 12.0% threshold).
points.note: Summary!D37 used GEOMEAN >= 12 for everybody while the Analyze sheet asks for 15%. Both are shown.

points.title: Consistently high return on total capital (12% or better)
points.formula: AVERAGE(ROCE[0..9])  >=  12%      (for banks: ROA >= 1% and ROE >= 12%)
points.value: 10-year mean ROCE of 47.32% and mean ROA of 1.37% - clears the 12% hurdle.
points.note: Group 3 - ROE is slightly going down (e.g. 15% to 13%), not a dramatic decrease. Look at ROCE: we notice a small increase (e.g. 20% to 21%) and higher than ROE. Two possibilities theoretically: (1) a negative leverage - the company is borrowing at a rate higher than ROCE; (2) the company has a negative net financial debt, i.e. more cash than debt, and may be investing part of its cash at other projects which gets a lower return, so the ROE is going down. This is a strong signal to shareholders, who should push management either to find good investment opportunities or give it back through dividends.

points.title: Conservatively financed
points.formula: Years to pay off long-term debt  =  Borrowings / Net Profit   (pass if <= 5 years)   |   for banks/NBFCs: ROA >= 1% (borrowings are the lending inventory)
points.value: This is a lending institution (bank/NBFC): its borrowings are the lending inventory the business earns its spread on, so the debt-payoff clock in the calculation above is not the Buffettology test here. The inventory is judged by profitability instead - Mean ROA 1.37% clears the 1% bar.
points.note: The original statement5.py used df_bs.iloc[7] which is the TOTAL of the balance sheet (liabilities + equity), not Borrowings (df_bs.iloc[5]). The correct ratio is shown above. For financial institutions the score comes from the ROA-based lending test.

points.title: Actively buying back its shares
points.formula: Yes if Shares[n] < Shares[0]  (or  Shares[n-1] < Shares[1])
points.value: No - the share count has not fallen over the period.

points.title: Can the company repurchase shares to investors' advantage?
points.formula: Qualitative - can the buyback be sustained from free cash flow?
points.value: Free-cash-flow test for buybacks: compare the 10-year mean CFO/Net profit and CapEx/Net profit figures on this card. A company that converts profit into cash and needs little maintenance capex can fund buybacks for years; a cash-hungry business will issue shares instead.
points.note: Engine's cash-conversion check scored 1 (mean CFO/NP 327.64%, mean FCF/NP 317.77%).

points.title: Can the company increase prices along with inflation?
points.formula: Annualised price CAGR over 20 years  =  ((Price_now / Price_20y_ago)^(1/20) - 1) * 100   (pass if >= 4%)
points.value: Pricing power: the TI BA-35 widget in the Valuation tab solves this exactly - enter the price twenty years ago as PV, today's price as FV, N = 20 and hit CPT i. A number of 4% or more means the business can raise prices along with inflation; a negative number means you are looking at a price-competitive business and should move on.

points.title: Right operational costs (low maintenance capex)
points.formula: Maintenance capex  =  CapEx / Net Profit   (low is good: <= 50%)   |   CapEx as % of sales   |   for banks/NBFCs: heavy plant capex is not required
points.value: This is a lending institution: loans are its 'production line', so heavy plant & equipment capex is not required to stay in business (mean CapEx 13.05% of net profit). The operational-cost test therefore passes provided lending itself stays profitable - Mean ROA 1.37% - and cash conversion (mean CFO/Net profit 327.64%) remains healthy.

points.title: Market panic, business recession or curable individual calamity
points.formula: Curable calamity if price is >= 15% below its 3-year high, or the P/E is below its 10-year average
points.value: Curable calamity: check the drawdown from the 3-year high and the P/E against its own 10-year average. A business that is temporarily out of favour (bad quarter, sector scare, one-off write-off) is exactly where Buffettology wants you to be buying.

points.title: Initial rate of return vs US Treasury bonds
points.formula: Initial Rate of Return %  =  (Current EPS / Current Price) * 100
points.value: Initial rate of return 5.4% with expected growth 13.28% against a risk-free rate of 6.8% - the combination does not clear the risk-free hurdle.

points.title: Stock's value relative to Treasury bonds
points.formula: Relative Value  =  Initial Rate of Return %  /  Risk-free Rate %
points.value: The stock does NOT offer better value than the risk-free asset.
points.note: Computation!F7 = F3/F5/100 divides the raw EPS by the treasury rate expressed in percent, which is dimensionally wrong; the correct Relative Value is (EPS/Price) / treasury-rate.

points.title: Projected annual compounding return as an equity/bond (Book Value model)
points.formula: Book Value Growth % = ROE% * (1 - Payout%/100)  ->  BV in 10Y = BV_now * (1+g)^10  ->  EPS in 10Y = BV_10Y * ROE%/100  ->  Price in 10Y = EPS_10Y * Terminal P/E  ->  Intrinsic Value = Price_Projected_10Y / (1 + r)^10  ->  Compounding return = ((Price_10Y / Price_now)^(1/10) - 1) * 100
points.value: Projected annual compounding return from the Book Value Equity/Bond model: see the Valuation tab. Intrinsic value 1879.45 against a current price of 1403.0 (+34.0%).

points.title: Projected return using historical per-share earnings growth / Intrinsic Value
points.formula: EPS_10Y = EPS_now * (1 + min(EPS CAGR, 18%))^10  ->  Price_10Y = EPS_10Y * Terminal P/E  ->  Intrinsic Value = Price_10Y / (1 + r)^10  ->  Compounding return = ((Price_10Y/P_now)^(1/10)-1)*100
points.value: Historical-EPS-growth model intrinsic value: see the Valuation tab. Compare the two models with the third (bond-coupon) model before you commit - they use different assumptions.

points.title: Are share prices and book value on the rise?

points.title: Earnings-per-share growth-rate test (5 year vs 10 year)
points.formula: 5Y EPS growth rate  vs  full-span EPS growth rate: pass if 5Y >= 12% (competitive benchmark), or 5Y >= full-span with positive growth (acceleration test), or 5Y Net Profit CAGR >= 12% with EPS growth positive (IPO-dilution rescue)
points.value: 5Y EPS CAGR 56.89% against the full-span CAGR of 16.19% (5Y Net Profit CAGR 42.06%). Earnings growth MEETS the >=12% competitive benchmark or the acceleration test.

points.title: Is revenue growth accelerating or decelerating? Did profits improve?
points.formula: Accelerating if 5Y Revenue CAGR > full-span Revenue CAGR (with positive growth); pass outright if the 5Y or full-span Revenue CAGR >= 12%; 'Decelerating' + profits improved if 5Y EPS growth > full-span EPS growth
points.value: Accelerating - 5Y revenue CAGR 15.99% vs full-span 7.41% (EPS: 5Y 56.89%, full-span 16.19%).
points.note: A company compounding revenue at 12%+ across ANY available span passes this checkpoint - a short listed history (e.g. a recent IPO) is no longer reported as 'Insufficient data'.

points.title: Consistently earning a high return (15% or better) on equity
points.formula: GEOMEAN(ROE[0..9])  >=  15%   (12% for banks and other financial institutions)

points.title: Consistently high return on total capital (12% or better)

points.title: Conservatively financed

points.formula: Qualitative - can the buyback be sustained from free cash flow?

points.title: Can the company increase prices along with inflation?

points.title: Right operational costs (low maintenance capex)

points.title: Stock's value relative to Treasury bonds

points.value: Pricing power: the TI BA-35 widget in the Valuation tab solves this exactly - enter the price twenty years ago as PV, today's price as FV, N = 20 and hit CPT i. A number of 4% or more means the business can raise prices along with inflation; a negative number means you are looking at a price-competitive business and should move on.

points.title: Right operational costs (low maintenance capex)
points.formula: Maintenance capex  =  CapEx / Net Profit   (low is good: <= 50%)   |   CapEx as % of sales   |   for banks/NBFCs: heavy plant capex is not required
points.value: This is a lending institution: loans are its 'production line', so heavy plant & equipment capex is not required to stay in business (mean CapEx 65.85% of net profit). The operational-cost test therefore passes provided lending itself stays profitable - Mean ROA 5.25% - and cash conversion (mean CFO/Net profit 163.54%) remains healthy.

points.title: Market panic, business recession or curable individual calamity
points.formula: Curable calamity if price is >= 15% below its 3-year high, or the P/E is below its 10-year average
points.value: Curable calamity: check the drawdown from the 3-year high and the P/E against its own 10-year average. A business that is temporarily out of favour (bad quarter, sector scare, one-off write-off) is exactly where Buffettology wants you to be buying.

points.title: Initial rate of return vs US Treasury bonds
points.formula: Initial Rate of Return %  =  (Current EPS / Current Price) * 100
points.value: Initial rate of return (earnings yield) versus the risk-free rate: the price you pay determines your return. Both the earnings yield and the expected growth rate should beat the risk-free rate; if the treasuries look juicier, the stock is overpriced.

points.title: Stock's value relative to Treasury bonds
points.formula: Relative Value  =  Initial Rate of Return %  /  Risk-free Rate %
points.value: The stock does NOT offer better value than the risk-free asset.
points.note: Computation!F7 = F3/F5/100 divides the raw EPS by the treasury rate expressed in percent, which is dimensionally wrong; the correct Relative Value is (EPS/Price) / treasury-rate.

points.title: Projected annual compounding return as an equity/bond (Book Value model)
points.formula: Book Value Growth % = ROE% * (1 - Payout%/100)  ->  BV in 10Y = BV_now * (1+g)^10  ->  EPS in 10Y = BV_10Y * ROE%/100  ->  Price in 10Y = EPS_10Y * Terminal P/E  ->  Intrinsic Value = Price_Projected_10Y / (1 + r)^10  ->  Compounding return = ((Price_10Y / Price_now)^(1/10) - 1) * 100
points.value: Not enough data to complete the Book Value Equity/Bond model for this company.

points.title: Projected return using historical per-share earnings growth / Intrinsic Value
points.formula: EPS_10Y = EPS_now * (1 + min(EPS CAGR, 18%))^10  ->  Price_10Y = EPS_10Y * Terminal P/E  ->  Intrinsic Value = Price_10Y / (1 + r)^10  ->  Compounding return = ((Price_10Y/P_now)^(1/10)-1)*100
points.value: Not enough data to complete the historical-EPS-growth model for this company.

company_type.detail: At least one year in the window had non-positive EPS, so future earnings cannot be predicted with confidence.

roe_roce_group.label: Group 2
roe_roce_group.detail: ROE (9.33%) and ROCE (12.2%) are close or moving together (trends: ROE increasing, ROCE increasing; gap -2.87 points) - the operational return is driving equity performance.
roe_roce_group.comment: Group 2 - It shows a very stable ROE which is very satisfactory. ROCE is stable too and equal to ROE. This means there's no debt: everything is coming from operations. Not only is the company very safe, it also has great flexibility for the future. The company can use its debt potential to face some of its temporary problems.

points.title: Durable Competitive Advantage
points.formula: Qualitative - supported by the quantitative evidence in points 5.2, 6, 7, 8 and 12
points.value: The Coca-Cola Company, a beverage company, manufactures and sells various nonalcoholic beverages in the United States and internationally. The Coca-Cola Company operates in Beverages - Non-Alcoholic (Consumer Defensive). Over the last decade it compounded per-share earnings at 6.01% a year while averaging a 34.98% return on equity and a 26.61% return on capital employed - that is the quantitative shape of a durable competitive advantage.
points.note: The narrative above is generated from the company's own business description and the financial ratios. Edit it to put it in your own words (Warren's test: explain it to a seven-year-old).

points.title: Brand-name product or key service
points.formula: Qualitative - habit / CRAP brand check, cross-referenced with 5.2, 6, 7, 8
points.value: Brand / habit check: this is a qualitative call. Use the evidence on this page: a stable or expanding operating margin, a high return on capital employed and a rising book value are the quantitative fingerprints of a habit-forming product or a must-have service. The company's own description is pasted at Point 1.
points.note: (AI offline - scored from the margin/ROE fingerprint: 1).

points.title: Organised labour force (union)
points.formula: Qualitative - organised labour check
points.value: Union check: this is a qualitative call. Banks, PSU banks, IT services and heavy-manufacturing utilities are the ones to check first; capital-light consumer brands rarely are.
points.note: AI offline - scored from the sector mix (1 = no organised-labour dependence: 1). Edit or click YES/NO to override.

points.title: Do you understand how the product works?
points.formula: Qualitative - can you explain the product in one sentence?
points.value: Can you explain how the product works and how the customer pays in one sentence? The engine cannot answer that for you - it can only remind you that if you cannot explain it, you should forget it and find a business you do understand.
points.note: AI offline - scored from the available business description (1). Edit to put it in your own words.

points.title: Chance of obsolescence in the next 20 years
points.formula: Qualitative - 20-year obsolescence risk
points.value: 20-year obsolescence: use the 10-year revenue and margin trend. A business whose revenue still compounds and whose operating margin is stable after a decade has usually survived one technology cycle already; that is evidence, not proof.
points.note: AI offline - scored from the revenue/profit CAGR trend (1).

points.title: Allocates capital exclusively in the realm of its expertise
points.formula: Total Retained Earnings Grown in %  =  (EPS[now] - EPS[10y ago]) / (Total 10Y EPS - Total 10Y Dividends) * 100
points.value: Return on retained earnings of 43.11% vs a risk-free rate of 4.98% - the company creates value from the earnings it retains.
points.note: Equivalent to statement4.py's calculate_earnings_growth() and to Computation!B10 in the template.

points.title: Predicting earnings at a glance (Company I / II / III / IV)
points.formula: Company IV if EPS[now] < 0; else Company I if all EPS > 0 and EPS[now] >= EPS[n-1]; else Company III if all EPS > 0; else Company II
points.value: Company I - Durable Competitive Advantage - Per-share earnings are consistently positive and the latest year is at or above the prior year: the 'perfect situation' Buffettology looks for.
points.note: Exhibit A (the two images embedded in the Analyze sheet).

points.title: Do earnings show a strong upward trend?
points.formula: 10Y EPS growth rate  =  ((EPS[n]/EPS[0])^(1/n) - 1) * 100     [average of YoY growth % as a cross-check]
points.value: Per-share earnings compounded at 6.01% a year over the available 11-year span, against a risk-free rate of 4.98%.
points.note: The original statement5.py printed the MEAN OF THE RAW EPS RUPEES as the 'growth rate' (e.g. '10-year average EPS growth rate is: 150%' for a stock with EPS of 150). The correct figure is the compound growth rate shown above.

points.title: Are share prices and book value on the rise?
points.formula: Current Price > earliest comparable price   AND   Book Value growth rate > 0
points.value: Share price is above its level 10 years ago; book value is growing.

points.title: Earnings-per-share growth-rate test (5 year vs 10 year)
points.formula: 5Y EPS growth rate  vs  full-span EPS growth rate: pass if 5Y >= 12% (competitive benchmark), or 5Y >= full-span with positive growth (acceleration test), or 5Y Net Profit CAGR >= 12% with EPS growth positive (IPO-dilution rescue)
points.value: 5Y EPS CAGR 7.81% against the full-span CAGR of 6.01% (5Y Net Profit CAGR 7.62%). Earnings growth MEETS the >=12% competitive benchmark or the acceleration test.
points.note: Summary!D30 compared the two values as TEXT ('5.48 %' vs '0.44 %'), which compares alphabetically. Here they are compared as numbers, and a >12% 5Y CAGR passes outright.

points.title: Is revenue growth accelerating or decelerating? Did profits improve?
points.formula: Accelerating if 5Y Revenue CAGR > full-span Revenue CAGR (with positive growth); pass outright if the 5Y or full-span Revenue CAGR >= 12%; 'Decelerating' + profits improved if 5Y EPS growth > full-span EPS growth
points.value: Accelerating - 5Y revenue CAGR 5.53% vs full-span 1.52% (EPS: 5Y 7.81%, full-span 6.01%).
points.note: A company compounding revenue at 12%+ across ANY available span passes this checkpoint - a short listed history (e.g. a recent IPO) is no longer reported as 'Insufficient data'.

points.title: Consistently earning a high return (15% or better) on equity
points.formula: GEOMEAN(ROE[0..9])  >=  15%   (12% for banks and other financial institutions)
points.value: 10-year geometric-average return on equity of 32.12% (above the 15.0% threshold).
points.note: Summary!D37 used GEOMEAN >= 12 for everybody while the Analyze sheet asks for 15%. Both are shown.

points.title: Consistently high return on total capital (12% or better)
points.formula: AVERAGE(ROCE[0..9])  >=  12%      (for banks: ROA >= 1% and ROE >= 12%)
points.value: 10-year mean ROCE of 26.61% and mean ROA of 8.87% - clears the 12% hurdle.
points.note: Group 3 - ROE is slightly going down (e.g. 15% to 13%), not a dramatic decrease. Look at ROCE: we notice a small increase (e.g. 20% to 21%) and higher than ROE. Two possibilities theoretically: (1) a negative leverage - the company is borrowing at a rate higher than ROCE; (2) the company has a negative net financial debt, i.e. more cash than debt, and may be investing part of its cash at other projects which gets a lower return, so the ROE is going down. This is a strong signal to shareholders, who should push management either to find good investment opportunities or give it back through dividends.

points.title: Conservatively financed

points.value: Conservatively financed: long-term debt could be retired in 2.71 years of current net earnings.
points.note: The original statement5.py used df_bs.iloc[7] which is the TOTAL of the balance sheet (liabilities + equity), not Borrowings (df_bs.iloc[5]). The correct ratio is shown above.
